body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Near-peer versus faculty teaching of clinical examination skills: a randomised comparison of OSCE performance","authors":"Okoro-Lindberg F, Delacroix-Mensah P, Watanabe-Hurst G","year":2018,"venue":"Journal of Clinical Skills Education","doi":"10.5555/jcse.2018.0144","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 124 second-year medical students to four examination-skills sessions taught either by trained final-year students or by faculty clinicians. The outcome was performance on four examination stations of the end-of-year OSCE, marked by examiners unaware of allocation. Station pass rates were 88 percent after near-peer teaching and 86 percent after faculty teaching, and the mean station score difference was 0.9 points in favour of near-peer teaching (95 percent CI -1.8 to 3.6). Students rated both formats highly, and near-peer tutors reported more confidence in their own examination technique. The study was at one school and too small to show a difference of less than 10 percentage points in pass rates."},{"title":"Near-peer teaching in undergraduate medical education: a systematic review of learner and tutor outcomes","authors":"Harrow-Adeyemi S, Kristensen-Obi T, Mahlaba-Ruiz C, Petersen-Kaur A","year":2021,"venue":"Medical Education Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/meer.2021.0209","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We searched four databases to 2020 for studies comparing near-peer with faculty teaching in undergraduate medicine. We included 32 studies, of which 7 were randomised. Most studies reported similar or better learner performance after near-peer teaching, but outcomes were heterogeneous and usually measured immediately after teaching. Learner satisfaction was high in almost all studies. Tutors reported gains in knowledge and teaching skills. Only 4 studies reported costs, and none valued the time of student tutors. The review concludes that near-peer teaching is at least comparable for skills teaching but that economic evidence is sparse."},{"title":"Costs of near-peer and faculty-led clinical skills teaching at one medical school: a cost comparison","authors":"Lemieux-Otieno B, Sorensen-Diallo K","year":2023,"venue":"Health Professions Education Finance","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We costed one academic year of examination-skills teaching at a medical school from the school's perspective. Faculty-led teaching cost 46 currency units per student contact hour, mainly sessional fees, and near-peer teaching cost 11 units per student contact hour, including tutor training, tutor payments and supervision. When the time of student tutors was valued at the rate paid for research assistant work, the near-peer cost rose to 19 units. Room and simulated patient charges were the same for both formats. The analysis did not measure learning outcomes, so it cannot say whether the cheaper option was equally effective."},{"title":"Self-selection into optional near-peer sessions and OSCE results: an analysis of three student years","authors":"Achebe-Lindqvist M, Farrow-Nakamura J, Osei-Brandt L","year":2020,"venue":"Assessment in Medical Education","doi":"10.5555/amed.2020.0063","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We examined 510 students across three years in which near-peer examination-skills sessions were optional. Students who attended had higher first-year assessment scores than those who did not. The unadjusted difference in OSCE examination-station scores between attenders and non-attenders was 5.2 points, which shrank to 1.1 points after adjustment for first-year scores and sex. Attendance was lowest among students who commuted long distances. The authors caution that comparisons based on optional attendance mainly reflect who chooses to attend, and recommend allocation by timetable or randomisation for future evaluations."},{"title":"What final-year tutors gain from near-peer teaching: an interview study","authors":"Quigley-Mbatha R, Oyelaran-Holt D","year":2016,"venue":"Journal of Peer Learning in Medicine","doi":"10.5555/jplm.2016.0021","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 18 final-year medical students who had tutored second-years in examination skills. Tutors described consolidating their own knowledge, learning to give feedback and growing confidence in front of groups. Several described time pressure in the months before their final examinations and asked for sessions to be scheduled earlier in the year. Some tutors felt unsure how far to correct technique that differed from what faculty had taught them. The authors recommend a short training course, a teaching guide aligned with faculty expectations and a limit on tutoring hours before finals."},{"title":"Detection of examination technique errors by near-peer and faculty tutors: an observational comparison","authors":"Varga-Okonjo T, Lindgren-Assefa H, Brooks-Ishikawa N","year":2025,"venue":"Clinical Teaching Quality","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We video-recorded 60 small-group examination-skills sessions, 30 led by near-peer tutors and 30 by faculty, and compared the errors in student technique that tutors corrected with those identified by two independent reviewers. Near-peer tutors left 22 percent of technique errors uncorrected compared with 12 percent for faculty tutors. The difference was largest for cardiovascular and neurological examinations. After a one-hour calibration session for tutors, the proportion of errors missed by near-peer tutors fell to 15 percent. Sessions were at one school and tutors knew they were being recorded."}]}
